posts.c: Jolene Kao bought Charlotte’s iconic Old Brick Store in 2023, determined to revive the historic building as a bustling local hub, where people could shop, eat, and connect with friends and strangers alike. She installed an espresso bar, freshened up the menu of prepared food and began stocking the shelves with specialty goods in addition to classic kitchen staples. Kao also brought back something the store lacked in recent years: seating, with a long farmhouse table and stools along a coffee counter. The changes paid off. The store now hums throughout the day as workers drop by for breakfast or lunch, families pop in for milk or eggs, and visitors linger over coffee. But not everyone is celebrating the newfound energy. ✍️ Colin Flanders 📸 @hanks.pix
posts.hd: Neighbor dispute over Old Brick Store roils Charlotte

posts.c: 🦬 Hudson Freeman w/ James Eichman | Friday, May 21 🎫 On sale 11.13 at 10 _ Welcome to Doom Country. We’ve been waiting for you. The new album from Hudson Freeman arrives, shattering any listeners’ malaise. Freeman delivers a post-rapture roadtrip album for the ages. Unshakeable riffs, philosophical explorations, and one heavy-ass band at his back. It’s a new high for the Brooklyn-based indie artist. A gorgeous record that weaves the intimate story telling of Andy Shauf, the expansive production of Arcade Fire’s The Suburbs, and the unflinching yet tasteful power of Wednesday's Rat Saw God. Fitting together into one stunning LP that introduces the world to Freeman’s ever-evolving sound. The record finds Freeman digging deeper into the sounds he’s most excited by, using them to spend time with the ideas that he’s most curious to understand. A band who has found and forged the heart of these songs on the road together, a team of collaborators willing to experiment sonically and live left

posts.c: Saying that he’s “gonna have to keep an eye on that one,” Ohio State University resident assistant Scott Joachim confirmed Wednesday that he is “not getting a good vibe” from the freshman student on his floor who wears a cloak at all times. “It’s hard enough being a freshman in the first weeks of school and trying to find your identity, but on top of all that this kid’s gotta throw a cloak in the mix?” said Joachim of the 18-year old student who is reportedly registered under the name Tim Estrin but, on the rare occasions that he has spoken with hallmates, has introduced himself only as “Damien.” “And he’s not wearing the cloak in a humorous, quirky way, either. He’s clearly dead serious. Everyone in the whole dorm just calls him Cloak Kid.” At press time, a relieved Joachim saw the student entering his room with a young woman who was also wearing a cloak.

posts.c: 🚨 BREAKING: Introducing X-70 Fractal, @nasa’s newest experimental aircraft! This crewed, modular aircraft will allow the agency to rapidly swap out internal & external payloads to help keep pushing the frontiers of aviation technology! X-70 Fractal is a high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight. “We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.” - @nasaadmin The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions. Details: nasa.gov/aero Image caption: Gener

posts.c: It’s about time we talked about this… This tall clock was made by Thomas Wagstaffe, a renowned Quaker clockmaker based in London. It’s also one of the oldest objects in the collection at @hamptonnps, originally commissioned in 1760 by Captain Charles Ridgely. That means it’s been keeping track of time for more than 260 years, give or take. You might say it’s been around the clock a few times. Clocks like this are often called grandfather clocks, and this one is an eight-day clock, meaning it can keep ticking for eight days on a single winding. That’s a full week of punctuality, plus a day of grace. Even clocks appreciate a long weekend. Not bad for something made before electricity or smartphones. Of course, there’s a catch. The clock still needs to be wound regularly, or it will eventually run out of time. Video shows a curator wearing gloves as they carefully wind the historic clock. The sound of the winding mechanism and the clock’s chimes can be heard. NPS.
posts.hd: 1760 tall clock by Thomas Wagstaffe at Hampton

posts.c: What is Stick Season? Aside from being the title of a popular song by Vermont singer-songwriter Noah Kahan, this "mini season" has a reputation for being a gloomy time of year. It's the period of time after fall foliage has fallen and before winter snow arrives, and is often overlooked for its lack of bright leaves or classic winter beauty. But what some folks don't know is that some of the best hiking happens during Stick Season! posts.c: If you recognize this funky little seed in the first place, you may be wondering why you haven't seen too many of them this fall... Well, we have answers! The results of our annual survey of tree nuts (called "hard mast" by foresters) looking at the crop of beech nuts, pictured here, and acorns state-wide are in: 2026 was a spotty year. Except for a few isolated sites high in the mountains and far to the north, most beech stands in Vermont saw total crop failure. Acorn production was more variable, with some sites yielding bumper crops and others just a stone's throw away yielding very little. Generally speaking, northern Vermont had a rough acorn year while southern and central Vermont faired better. It should be noted that none of this is cause for alarm! Mast production naturally cycles year to year and species to species. Wildlife like deer, turkey, bears and squirrels that depend on beech nuts and acorns in this part of their range have adapted accordingly. What this does mean is

posts.c: New Mexico elected @debhaalandnm as governor in the 2026 midterm elections, making her the first female Native American governor-elect in U.S. history. It’s a milestone in a career marked by historic firsts. From 2021 to 2025, Haaland served as the first Indigenous U.S. Secretary of the Interior, overseeing the nation’s public lands and national parks. As a member of the Pueblo of Laguna tribe, she brought a particular focus to protecting Indigenous lands and honoring their cultural significance. In 2023, Haaland was featured in our annual @womenwhotravel Power List, where she reminded travelers that to understand a destination means understanding its history: “If you are visiting another state, another county, another city, research that place. What tribes lived there prior to colonization? What tribes still live there?” You can read the full interview and find the 2023 Women Who Travel Power List at the link in bio.

posts.c: Peak cycle! A flashback from my cycle test 5 days after return to Earth from the @iss. A mask collects the air we exhale to measure the amount of CO2 we exhale (our metabolic rate), and electrodes measure our heart rate and rhythm. Our scientists and doctors use these data to ensure all is well with our cardiovascular snd respiratory systems. Just 5 days after landing and I exceeded my performance from my last test before the flight! Yet another indication that our exercise equipment on the ISS not only maintains, but can increase our fitness level even while in microgravity.

posts.c: In Spring 2027, @belmond's Venice Simplon-Orient-Express (@vsoetrain) is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history. The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality. A journey aboard @belmond's luxe Venice-Simplon Orient Express is on many travelers’ bucket lists. After settling into a sophisticated cabin on the Art Deco-era train, passengers are ushered into one of the opulent dining cars—complete with velvet seats and glossy marquetry—for four-course dinners prepared with seasonal ingredients. The highlight, however, are the festive evenings in the train’s bar car, named 3674. There, guests turn out in their finest black tie attire for a night of live piano music and specialty cocktails in the historic lounge. At the link in bio, learn more about how to boo

posts.c: If you have a room you don’t like, try making small changes over time! 🎀✨🩵 When we first redid our kitchen in 2021, I’d added some color, but mostly went with the “a white kitchen is timeless” advice. Turns out, I like living with more color! So over time I slowly added it, mostly in the form of paint. It was one small tweak at a time. No huge renovation. And I loved being able to slowly bring the space together! So if you have a room that bugs you? Change one thing. Live with it. Then change the next thing. Simple, but I promise you it works! How do you like the new yellow ceiling? 💛 Paint colors- Yellow- Sweet as Honey Pink- Beloved Pink Mint- Frosted Sage (All by Behr)

posts.c: It’s leaf-peeping season. The trees have made an effort, so the least we can do is go outside and stare at them. Leaf peeping is the ancient human tradition of traveling long distances to look at leaves, take photographs, and stand in the middle of roads while saying, “Oh, wow, look at that one.” Nobody knows exactly when this became a major event, but the trees seem okay with the arrangement. So get out there and see what all the rustle is about. NPS photos: @zionnps @nationalmallnps @greatsmokynps @greatsmokynps @shenandoahnps @grandtetonnps @indianadunesnps @sleepingbearnps Cowpens

posts.c: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own. As we get closer to the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a long list of science objectives await. One way Roman will team up with Hubble is by the different ways the missions will study exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Roman will likely find hundreds of thousands exoplanets with its remarkable instruments; meanwhile, Hubble’s capabilities allow for analysis of exoplanet atmospheres. This work is part of NASA's search for life elsewhere in the universe. Plus, Roman's coronograph instrument will be able to directly image some larger exoplanets. We'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy in the weeks to come. Check the link in our bio for more on Hubble and Roman! Image description: A collage of artistic renderings of differently colored exoplanets in rows, against a black background. In the lower left, faint text reads

posts.c: Each Tuesday this season, we're sharing stories that highlight what Rock Point means to you! "Access to the beauty and serenity that nature provides is critical for my mental health, and I have turned to Rock Point many times over the years for its ability to calm my body and recenter myself. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, I brought my kids there for walks on a daily basis, which proved to be one of the most grounding consistent experiences that helped us find peace during extremely uncertain times. And for the past five years, my organization, Dad Guild, has accessed Rock Point on a monthly basis for its Fires with Fathers program, which provides dads and masculine-identifying caregivers with space to connect with one another on a deeper level while practicing active listening and modeling vulnerability. Rock Point is my favorite location in all of Burlington, and I cannot imagine living in this community without it." -Keegan Albaugh, Executive Director, Dad Guild Have a testimonia

posts.c: You may notice that faces are back in my feed. After much feedback from clients and followers, there was a strong desire to see the full image when sharing images. posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. The largest was a Magnitude 2.0. Throughout 2026, there has been very little change in ground

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. posts.c: Hidden beauty 💛 Agorastos Papatsanis (@agorastospapatsanis) uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log. On the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, Agorastos experimented with ultraviolet (UV) illumination until it revealed the strongest fluorescent response from these mushrooms known as ‘beautiful bonnets’. While humans cannot see UV light, we can get an inkling of its effect, thanks to the phenomenon of fluorescence. Mycologists are harnessing this phenomenon to distinguish closely related species of fungi by the colours and patterns they reveal under UV. 📸 'Shedding Light' is the winner of #WPY62's Plants and Fungi category. posts.c: In this final video in our explainer series about the new deer hunting regulations this year, our Deer and Moose Project Leader Nick Fortin and Sergeant Dana Joyal from the Vermont Warden Service break down what is needed to legally take a doe in the upcoming rifle season. In order to legally take a doe during rifle season, you must have received an antlerless permit designated for a specific wildlife management unit (WMU). If you do not have a permit, you may not take a doe during the rifle season. If a hunter is unsuccessful during the rifle season, they may use that antlerless permit during the conventional muzzleloader season. Visit our website for more information about taking a doe during rifle season and all the new deer regulation changes.

posts.c: Where's the oxygen? After researchers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, they realized much of the oxygen they expected to see was missing. Oxygen is the main element formed by stars, and also the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium. But by using Hubble, these scientists learned that dwarf galaxies can only hang on to a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. Energy from the low-mass galaxies’ massive stars, along with galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions, are apparently more effective at driving out the oxygen than current models predict. Read more at the link in our bio! Día de los Muertos has its roots in an Aztec ritual known as Miccaihuitl, honoring those who have passed. The celebration coincides with the return of monarch butterflies that typically flutter away from our region and make the long flight back to Mexico to spend their winter in a warmer climate. Believed to carry the souls of the departed returning to visit their families, it’s easy to see why these beautiful, winged messengers are held sacred by so many Indigenous communities along their path. 🌼🌼🌼 El Día de los Muertos tiene sus raíces en un antiguo ritual Azteca llamado Miccaihuitl, en honor de los antepasados. Da la casualidad de que coincide con el retorno de las mariposas monarcas que típicamente vuelan de nuestra región al norte y emprenden el largo vuelo de regreso a México donde pasan el invierno en un clima más cálido. Se cree que llevan consigo las almas de los difuntos que vuelven a visitar a sus familias. Es fácil ver por qué estas mensajeras aladas se consideran sagradas

posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. posts.c: Have you seen a whale shark before? Alex Lindbloom’s (@alexlindbloomphoto) photo shows a whale shark investigating the catch of a 'bagan', or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He used the lights of the began to illuminate the sharks for his drone’s camera. Local fishing communities are using the predictable occurrence of whale sharks at bagans to attract tourists. Although contact with bagans can cause some minor injuries to whale sharks, this isn’t a major cause of mortality. Instead, the main reasons for the sharp decline in whale sharks in the Indo-Pacific region over the past 75 years are ship strikes, entanglements with fishing gear and illegal fishing. 📸 ‘Night-Time Catch’ is the winner of #WPY62's Oceans: The Bigger Picture category. posts.c: Star Wars became hugely popular because it combined an exciting adventure story with groundbreaking special effects. When George Lucas released the first film in 1977, audiences had rarely seen space battles, alien worlds, and futuristic technology portrayed so convincingly. Its memorable characters, including Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, and Princess Leia, helped make the story appealing to audiences of all ages. Another major reason was its enormous cultural influence. Star Wars introduced iconic lightsabers, unforgettable music by John Williams, and a fictional universe that fans could explore through toys, books, games, and sequels. Its simple story of good versus evil made it easy to connect with, while its detailed universe kept fans interested for decades. It transformed science fiction from a relatively niche genre into mainstream entertainment. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Hats were once an essential part of everyday fashion because they served both practical and social purposes. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, men and women wore hats to protect themselves from sunlight, rain, and cold weather. Hats also symbolized respectability, social status, and good manners. Going outside without one was sometimes considered improper, especially on formal occasions. Hat-wearing declined dramatically during the mid-20th century as fashion became more casual, cars became widespread, and elaborate hairstyles grew popular. President John F. Kennedy is sometimes blamed for ending the hat trend, although it was already declining before his presidency. Interestingly, there was a time when leaving home without a hat could seem almost as unusual as leaving without shoes today. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: Pirates were far more organized than movies suggest, especially during the Golden Age of Piracy between the 1650s and 1730s. Many pirate crews elected their captains, voted on important decisions, and followed written rules. Some even had compensation systems for injured crew members. Interestingly, pirates rarely buried treasure, and the famous practice of making prisoners walk the plank was much less common than Hollywood suggests. Another surprising fact is that pirates sometimes used intimidation to avoid fighting altogether. The famous skull-and-crossbones flag, known as the Jolly Roger, warned ships to surrender before an attack. Pirates also included women, such as Anne Bonny and Mary Read, who became notorious in the early 18th century. Despite their reputation for lawlessness, some pirate crews operated with surprisingly democratic rules, at least among their own members. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

A big yawn mid-stretch makes for a deceptive image. Most of us are aware that wolves do not impersonate grannies to trick children or huff and puff houses to the ground. Still, the archetype of the “big bad wolf” persists in folklore and fiction. Fairy tales like Little Red Riding Hood seem harmless enough, but as biodiversity plummets across the world, suddenly the fictitious villain becomes a very real and very convenient scapegoat. When local wildlife begins to decline, predators are often unfairly blamed for the loss, despite the fact that habitat destruction and development play a much larger role. My hope in sharing the beauty of animals like wolves in my new book Reverence is to inspire empathy and encourage us to reevaluate how we coexist with our planet’s predators. Visit the link in my bio to get your copy.

Product reviews have a powerful influence on what people buy, with many shoppers trusting feedback from strangers almost as much as personal recommendations. Interestingly, products with a few negative reviews can sometimes appear more trustworthy than those with nothing but perfect ratings, because a flawless review history may seem suspicious. Another surprising fact is that people are more likely to leave reviews after extremely good or bad experiences than after ordinary ones. This can make online ratings less representative of the average customer’s experience. Fake reviews also complicate matters, which is why a detailed, balanced three-star review can sometimes tell you more than dozens of enthusiastic five-star ratings. Like this content? posts.c: Halloween is a time for things that go bump in the night. National parks have plenty of those. Boo! Still with us? From mysterious noises in the woods to wildlife that would prefer you keep your distance, the great outdoors can be downright spooky after dark. But the scariest encounters often have less to do with ghosts and more to do with poor planning, questionable decisions, and the occasional tree root working in cahoots with gravity. Whether you’re hiking a shadowy trail, camping beneath a full moon, or simply enjoying the autumn scenery, a few simple precautions can help keep your adventure from becoming a horror story. Stay on marked trails, watch your step, give wildlife plenty of space, check the weather, and pack the essentials. And if something in the woods starts whispering your name? Well, perhaps don’t investigate. Good luck! NPS

posts.c: This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. The tale of my spookiest adventure… and the only place I won’t hike again! 🔮✨ Deep in the hills above Eden is a section of the Long Trail known as Devil’s Gulch. You’d think a town named after the Garden of Eden wouldn’t have a haunted forest, but this is Vermont. Every forest is haunted… 🍂 In 1781, over 70 Green Mountain Boys were granted land here as a reward for fighting in the Revolution. Even though this area is stunning, none of them settled here. The hilly, rocky terrain offered little value for farming, and it was too removed from Vermont’s bustling towns. Whoever named this had a good sense of humor. At some point in Eden’s slow development, settlers found this ravine in the woods between Belvidere and Laraway Mountains. It became known as Devil’s Gulch, a term that dates back to the 1200s and means “to swallow greedily”. 🌿 This ravine is a defile, or place where the earth sort of burped, tossed up boulders, and dropped them in a jumble. These mossy, larger than life boulders

Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. Comment POKE below and we’ll send you the best tuna poke recipe from Chef @banchohajime of @sazanamirestaurant straight to your inbox! #NationalSeafoodMonth #PokeReci

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: I asked, you answered. These are the Vermont sayings that came up again and again when I asked my Facebook followers, “What’s a Vermont saying that you don’t hear anywhere else?” “Dooryard” won by a landslide, but that was never used in my family growing up here. My grandmother loved to say something “had the radish” right before she threw it in the trash. 10: Had the radish: Worn out, broken, done for 9: Grinder: A sub sandwich 8: Hard tellin’, not knowin’: I can’t say until I know more 7: Prit near: Pretty near, almost 6: Creemee: Soft-serve ice cream, ideally maple 5: Wicked: Very 4: Flatlander: Anyone not from Vermont 3: You can’t get there from here: The road you want doesn’t connect to the road you’re on. Turn left where the barn used to be. 2: Jeezum Crow: How Vermonters swear without actually swearing. 1: Dooryard: The yard right outside your door, where you park and the kids play. posts.c: 🍁 Peak fall color has entered the chat! We are officially calling it. The Gardens are gilded in autumn's incandescent glow. Golden oaks and tulip-trees light up Peirce’s Park. The Meadow Garden is a tapestry of auburn, amber, and rust. Everywhere you look, leaves and late-season blooms are reaching a glorious crescendo of color. And indoors, Chrysanthemum Festival is at peak bloom, adding an extraordinary flourish of color and artistry to the season. And like so many of nature’s most beautiful moments, this one is fleeting. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Here's something to warm your heart on a chilly fall day! These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

posts.c: Do you play Go? Simple rules. Endless possibilities. Over 2,500 years old, Go is a game where two players place black and white stones on a grid, competing to surround territory. It’s easy to learn the basics, with enough depth to keep you coming back for a lifetime. Remember Deep Blue beating chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997? It took almost two decades longer for AlphaGo to defeat Go legend Lee Sedol in 2016. That’s how much depth those little black and white stones hold. Roderick used to be big into Go, and he’s donated his board to Mesmer so you can enjoy it, too. Bring a friend, settle in, and play a game. And if Go isn’t your game, we have a full complement of other games to enjoy whenever we’re open. Come play. #kava #burlingtonvt #boardgames #go #nonalcoholic

posts.c: The original orange and black 🧡🖤 The San Diego Zoo and Safari Park care for two of the six tiger subspecies, Malayan and Sumatran. Sumatran tigers, native to the Indonesian island of Sumatra, are the smallest of the subspecies. Their darker coats help them blend into shadows, and longer fur on their faces may help protect them from dense vegetation. Malayan tigers, native to the forests of the Malay Peninsula, have a slightly lighter coat that complements their surroundings. #sandiegozoo #sdzsafaripark #tiger

posts.c: A few images from the chapter The Edge of Light in Reverence. I have been ice-obsessed since I was a kid crawling across the sea ice of the Arctic and running wild through the polar nights and endless summers. Every groove, crack, and dimple can be read like its own language, one I first learned from the Inuit elders of my hometown. What I did not know in those early days was how those skills would open entire worlds to me. They allowed me to delve deeper into the raw beauty of places like Antarctica and return with scenes I still dream of. posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: Each Tuesday this season, we're sharing stories that highlight what Rock Point means to you! "The cliffs rising over the Thrust Fault beach at Rock Point is one of the most beautiful places in Vermont! The stark juxtaposition of the dun colored Dolostone over the dark grey Iberville shale combined with the white cedars clinging to the cliffs is so dramatic. The fact that the top layer of rock is older than the bottom layer adds to the mystery. I have been leading trips to see this geologic feature for 40 years and it never ceases to amaze me and the people I am with. I always see wildlife at Rock Point from squirrels, foxes and mink to peregrines to ravens. Rock Point is a living sanctuary for people, plants and wild animals. It is truly the green heart of Burlington. I am so grateful to everyone who works to protect Rock Point's wild nature for us and for future generations." -Alicia Daniel, Director of Vermont Master Naturalist Have a testimonial you'd like to share? posts.c: 🦇 51 weeks of the year, bats are busy doing good by humans without many people ever realizing it. The last week of October, however, is that special 52nd week: Bat Week! That means it's time for us humans to say "thank you" to the bats! 🦇 If you're a professional bat biologist with Vermont Fish & Wildlife, every week is Bat Week, of course. The lucky few thank these glorious creatures by conducting cutting-edge telemetry research on their migratory patterns, or venturing deep underground to collect samples that will help us learn more about how bats are developing resilience against the devastating bat illness known as white-nose syndrome. But if you're not a bat biologist... what can YOU do for Bat Week? We recommend cleaning out your bat box! With bats leaving their summer roosts, you can tidy up a bat box at this time of year without worrying about disturbing the residents. Don't have a bat box? Well, you are in luck. Fall is a great time to pick a good spot and put up a bat box on

posts.c: The spirit bears of my new book Reverence. Over ten years ago, a @natgeo assignment sent me deep into the Great Bear Rainforest in search of the elusive spirit bear. At the time, big oil interests were pushing a pipeline from Canada’s Tar Sands to British Columbia, threatening the waterways that sustain the rainforest. First Nations communities were leading the fight against the project, and the magazine was after images that could rally the public behind them. Which is how I found myself crouched at the mossy edge of a cold stream, mesmerized as, just inches away, a spirit bear fished from the rushing waters. Under the guidance of @gitgaatspirit, I spent weeks in that mossy kingdom getting to know the wise little spirits that call it home. Soon after the story was finally published, the pipeline project was defeated. Reverence is now available in a limited print run, of which only a few thousand copies remain. posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. Different containers can change how quickly soil dries out, how much heat it holds, and how easily excess water escapes. B

posts.c: What can you do to support biodiversity in your forest? Thoughtful forest management plays an important role in supporting and promoting biodiversity. Even small actions make a difference. 🪵 Embrace Messiness: Leave dead and downed trees to provide essential shelter, food, and nesting sites for wildlife. 🌳 Grow Trees of Different Ages: A mix of tree ages creates diverse habitats and resilient forests. 🌿Encourage Plant Diversity: Create space for native species to grow and protect young trees from being browsed by deer. 🌲 Maintain Connected Habitat Areas: Allow plants, animals, and fungi to move freely between your forest and neighboring lands and habitats. Ready to learn more? Check out the @uvmextforestry's new Forest Biodiversity website for educational guides and stewardship resources. Developed in partnership with @audubonvermont, @vtcoverts, Vermont Biodiversity Alliance, @vtforestsparksrecreation, and @vwatreefarm. 🔗Link in bio! Illustration by Carmen McFadden @propheticnewt

posts.c: Ever look at all the rain hitting your roof and wonder how much water you’re letting go to waste? A rainwater capture system puts that water to work. Every inch of rain falling on a 1,000-square-foot roof can produce around 600 gallons of water. Gutters collect the runoff and direct it into a system that can help keep your garden watered. The science is all about collecting and filtering water before it reaches storage. A leaf filter catches larger debris, while a first flush diverter sends the dirtiest initial runoff away from the tank. This matters because dust, bird droppings, and other contaminants can build up on your roof between rainfalls. Removing that initial runoff helps keep your stored water cleaner. This rainwater capture system stores up to 5,750 gallons across the property, with underground pipes directing collected water into a main 5,000-gallon tank. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

posts.c: So @jacquesinthegarden stumbled across a mystery pomegranate tree growing near his house, and the fruit turned out to be the sweetest he’d ever tasted. The science comes down to genetics. Pomegranates grown from seed can have a unique combination of genes from their parent plants, so the fruit may taste completely different from what you’d expect. That’s why this mystery tree outperformed one he had intentionally grown for three years. If you find a pomegranate with incredible flavor, you’ll want to clone it rather than grow it from seed. Hardwood cuttings can develop roots and grow into genetically identical plants, preserving the traits that made the original fruit so good. Keeping those cuttings warm while providing indirect light can help encourage root development, especially during cooler weather. And here’s the fun part: birds like crows can spread seeds to new places, creating unexpected seedlings throughout a neighborhood. You might not know what you’re growing until it fruits

Narrowing the full gallery down to just a few select photos to share on Instagram was not easy! posts.c: We created a fleet of no-cost, seriously spooky, DIY witches brooms, with cuttings from our own yard.⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ Start by cutting small bundles of ornamental grass and hang them upside down to dry (you can skip the drying part). Cut branches to size (we got ours from our birch tree) and on one end wrap and knot twine - making sure to leave a 6” tail. Then, center the branch in a grass bundle before wrapping the grass with twine to keep it in place. Use the tail to tie off. Trim the grass to your desired length. Last, use a hook or just tie string around the other end of the branch to hang. ⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ We love the look and it was the perfect project to get us started on a very spooky exterior 🧙‍♀️⠀⠀ •⠀⠀ #renovationhusbands #diy #diydecor #halloween #halloweendecor diyhalloween

posts.c: Best of my time in west mt airy 🩷 the most magical cottagey rowhouse on the most charming street- I put a lot of love into this place to make it feel like home for me- painted the whole dang thing, replaced the light fixtures, planted a whole bunch of plants, and more! I enjoyed her for 2.5 years but it was time for change! I went through a big breakup here- my first and only relationship that lasted 8 years. I lived here alone for a year and a half, becoming a single cat mommy of two, while I healed and found my way back to myself, found new hobbies (tennis, rock climbing, knitting, golfing, following baseball again), prioritizing my friendships and making new ones, learning how to spend comfortable time alone and figure things out for myself after living with someone for so long. I imagine I’ll find my way back to mt airy since I love her so much, but for now I’m back in the city and excited to decorate my new solo (!!!) apt and for all that comes next 💖

posts.c: Brewing up new stars 🪄 @NASAWebb’s unique view of the stellar nursery known as NGC 7129 reveals numerous stars formerly hidden in this cosmic cauldron. Stars begin their life in cold, dense regions of dust and gas, hiding from view of most telescopes. Webb’s high degree of infrared sensitivity allows astronomers to peer through dust to study these baby stars. In this image, we can see stars in various stages of development. The most mature and massive (about 5-8x the mass of our Sun) is the region’s bright central star. In the cavity on the left, appearing in gold, is the largest demonstration of its impact. The outflows from an earlier stage in the star’s development carve into the dense molecular cloud of hydrogen, and combine with the star’s light, causing it to glow. The region on the right, represented in red, hides much younger objects than those on the left: protostars. posts.c: He’s changed your life with dogs, and now, he’d like to change your dog’s life. Tomorrow, Elias Weiss Friedman, a.k.a. @TheDogist, is launching a brand dedicated to pet wellness, @TheDogistCompany, starting with an antioxidant soft-chew supplement. “This was a type of product that didn’t exist,” Friedman tells Forbes Vetted’s managing editor (and resident pet expert) Emmy Favilla of the Vitality antioxidant supplement, noting that it aims to fill a gap in the market and take the place of a multivitamin. Formulated with Dr. Angela Rollins, a board-certified veterinary nutritionist and clinical professor at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (@utcvm), Vitality intends to reduce inflammation and support overall wellness, especially for picky eaters who aren’t eager for fruits and veggies, like Friedman’s own dog, Elsa. 🐶 The chew enters a market filled with pet multivitamins, which aren’t always a necessary addition to a dog’s diet. Today marks the beginning of a new chapter for The Dogist! 🎉I’m proud to announce the founding of @thedogistcompany and its first product: Vitality – Your dog’s daily dose of antioxidants (available at link in bio). Also featured today on @forbesvetted ! Elsa’s a picky eater (like many dogs), and refused to eat any healthy fruits or vegetables, like blueberries. This inspired me to partner with Dr. Angela Rollins, a Board Certified Veterinary Nutritionist (a rare speciality), to develop a new product that was different from any other dog health supplement on the market. We found that antioxidants, which help reduce oxidative stress on cells throughout the body, were missing from most fortified dog foods and supplements. Vitality was conceived, and after more than a year of development, it’s finally here! You can preorder your tin of Vitality right now at thedogistcompany.com! held.c: It is with profound sadness that we share the passing of our former Executive Director, John Killacky, who led the Flynn from 2010 to 2018. John brought to the Flynn a deep commitment to the arts as a force for connection, understanding, and social change. An artist, writer, and advocate, he built a career exploring questions of identity, disability, equity, and belonging. At the Flynn, he championed “Everybody Belongs,” a guiding principle of his leadership that remains visible on the walls of our building and woven into our mission today. John worked tirelessly to ensure that the Flynn welcomed everyone, expanding partnerships with community organizations and deepening the theatre’s connections across Vermont. He believed the arts should be accessible to all, regardless of ability, background, or circumstance, and pushed us to think more expansively about who belongs on our stages, in our audiences, and within our community. held.c: Ok people, It is Election Day and I hope you all know what that means! Time to go VOTE!! If you are like me, you may be saddened by the current political state in our country. Party allegiance aside, so much of what is being talked about seems to be fueled by hatred, violence and struggle. While It can all feel overwhelming, I always try and remember that the actual people who live in this country are loving, kind, hard working and resilient. When I was greeted with the above spread I was reminded about how great the people are and how important It is to elect leaders who think and act like us. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. Shoutout to whoever dialed in these cider doughnuts,

Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. held.c: Tomorrow! Wed 10/28. Join VSO Music Director Andrew Crust and James Stewart for drinks, snacks, and a casual tour of their October 31 concert. Three days before the Vermont Symphony Orchestra takes the stage at the Flynn, join VSO Music Director Andrew Crust and composer James Stewart at the Venetian Soda Lounge for a lively happy hour exploring the music on our October 31 program, The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. Andrew and James will discuss the composition process behind film scores from NOPE and The Nightmare Before Christmas, and explore how late-1800s compositions Symphonie fantastique and The Sorcerer’s Apprentice became enduring favorites. Sip your favorite drink, sample some charcuterie, ask questions, and discover why knowing the backstory makes the program even more unforgettable as we head towards the VSO’s Halloween matinee. What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,

held.c: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax. Rescued by PETA in 2010 at a year old, he was my shadow for the next 16+ years, sharing adventures and cuddles. His big brown eyes could stare into my soul and his big ears heard everything. He had quite the personality and loved to “talk,” and I quickly learned to understand his squeaks and groans. Jax was an excellent travel companion, happy to just be wherever I was. He was a master sunbather, always searching for the coziest spot in the house to catch some rays. In his younger years he loved to hike (and later enjoyed riding along in a backpack), and he was always ready to chase tennis balls or play tug-o’ -war until we were both exhausted. Then, he’d cuddle up next to me under a blanket, burrow his nose in, and snore and dream. At the end, with his face and muzzle nearly white, he was declining quickly and ready to go, and I was grateful to be able to give him a peaceful goodbye. Life isn’t the same without him,
held.cp: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax

This one is their New York record, a collection of songs about watching your hometown change and feeling the ways it has in turn changed you. Gather around the table on Thursday for an evening of good food and good wine. This ticketed, multi-course, family-style meal is a celebration the flavors of fall as part of @slowfoodvt Chicory Month. Featuring our pasture-raised pork, heirloom varieties of farm-grown chicories, and local apples from our friends and neighbors at @shelburneorchards, the menu will be complemented by special wine pairings from @jjpruem, one of Germany’s most celebrated Riesling producers. This family-owned estate in the Mosel is renowned for its elegant, beautifully balanced wines— a special opportunity to enjoy them alongside the autumn harvest here in Vermont. Meet the people behind the meal and hear the stories of what’s on the table. Philo Ridge Farm team members Ed Pitcavage and Jeremy LeClair will share more about the pork and chicories, Nick Cowles from Shelburne Orchards will talk about the apples, and Chris Corrao from @vinecyclewines will guide us through the wines. > > Tickets at link in bio.

held.c: 10 years ago today, we received a mention from a man named Brant. What followed was an interaction that has quite literally changed my life. Brant received a lot of criticism for his words that day, but 2016 was a different, more graceful internet, and he rolled with the punches. He wore the “they’re good dogs Brent” merch we sent him, his Simpson’s themed wedding cake featured Santa’s Little Helper holding a sign featuring the phrase, and best of all, 2 years later, Brant got a dog. Completing potentially the most wholesome, full circle meme to ever exist. We haven’t heard from him in a few years, but Brant, wherever you are, give Charlie a hug from us ❤️
